Based on the retrieved healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that admission to a tertiary care hospital may not necessarily improve survival for elderly patients with cardiogenic shock complicating acute myocardial infarction. In fact, a community-based cohort study found that patients admitted to tertiary centers did not have significantly different adjusted 30-day and 1-year mortality rates compared to those admitted to lower-level hospitals.

The study suggests that while admission to a tertiary center may be associated with lower short-term mortality among elderly patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, this benefit may be offset by differences in revascularization capabilities of the admitting hospital. Additionally, these studies do not provide evidence that tertiary centers provide better long-term outcomes or patient care.

Therefore, while admission to a tertiary center may have some benefits for elderly patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, it is not clear whether this translates to improved overall survival in this population. It is essential to note that individual patient circumstances and outcomes can vary widely, and more research is needed to fully understand the impact of admission to a tertiary center on long-term mortality for these patients.
